quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Tuck your bottom lip under your top teeth and stretch the first sound. With a fingertip resting on your lip, do you feel a tingle, or just smooth airflow?
quests.explanation: 'Fish' starts with /f/: the lower lip touches the upper teeth and air slides through the gap with your voice off, giving a quiet, smooth hiss. /v/ uses the identical lip-and-teeth position but adds a buzz, which you'd feel as a tickle on the lip.
quests.mouthPosition: Rest your upper teeth on your lower lip and breathe out steadily with your throat silent. Nothing should vibrate against your lip.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Lightly touch your bottom lip with a finger while you hold the first sound for three seconds. A tingle under your finger means the voice is on.
quests.explanation: 'Van' begins with /v/. The mouth shape is the same as for /f/, but the vocal cords vibrate and that vibration travels into the lip. Without it 'van' turns into 'fan', a common slip because the two sounds look identical from the outside.
quests.mouthPosition: Set your top teeth on your bottom lip, switch your voice on, and let the air buzz through the gap. Hold it a moment before moving to 'an'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Ignore the spelling, which starts with PH. In the first half-second, what are your lip and teeth doing, and is your voice on or off?
quests.explanation: 'Phone' begins with /f/ even though it's spelled PH; that spelling always signals /f/ in words like this. The lip touches the teeth, air hisses through, and the throat stays quiet. Since /v/ has the same mouth shape, the buzz is your only check.
quests.mouthPosition: Tuck your bottom lip under your top teeth and blow a smooth voiceless stream of air. Then round your lips for the 'oh'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Stretch the first sound for two seconds. Is it a clean hiss like air escaping a tyre, or a hiss with a hum running underneath?
quests.explanation: 'Soap' begins with /s/: tongue tip near the ridge, a narrow channel of air, and no voice at all. /z/ keeps the same tongue position and adds vibration, so 'soap' would become 'zoap'.
quests.mouthPosition: Bring your tongue tip close to the ridge behind your top teeth, spread your lips slightly, and blow a thin stream of air. Throat silent.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Block your ears with your fingers and stretch the first sound. One version will roar inside your head; the other stays thin.
quests.explanation: 'Zoo' starts with /z/. The tongue sits exactly where it does for /s/, but the vocal cords vibrate, which is why you hear it boom in your head with your ears covered. Many learners say 'soo' because word-initial /z/ is missing in some languages.
quests.mouthPosition: Set your tongue near the ridge as if for a hiss, then switch your voice on so the air buzzes across the tongue tip. Keep the buzz going before the 'oo'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The first letter is C, so don't lean on it. Stretch the first sound and feel whether your throat joins in.
quests.explanation: 'City' starts with /s/, because C stands for /s/ before I, E and Y. Hearing that voiceless hiss matters: if it drifts to /z/ the word becomes 'zitty'. Spelling suggests a sound, but your throat gives the verdict.
quests.mouthPosition: Hover your tongue tip near the ridge behind your upper teeth and push air through a thin channel with your throat quiet. Then relax into the short 'ity'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Listen to how long the vowel lasts before the last sound. Is it held out, or cut short and hissed away?
quests.explanation: 'Rice' ends in /s/. Vowels shorten before voiceless consonants, so the 'i' is brief and the word finishes on a clean hiss. 'Rise' ends in /z/, gets a longer vowel, and buzzes to the end. Learners often hold the voice too long and turn 'rice' into 'rise'.
quests.mouthPosition: End with your tongue tip near the ridge, pushing a thin voiceless stream of air. Stop the air cleanly instead of trailing off.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The spelling ends in S and E, but what is your throat doing as the word finishes? Stretch the ending and listen for a buzz.
quests.explanation: 'Please' ends in /z/ despite the S. The vowel is long and the buzz carries right into the last consonant. End on a hiss and you'll say 'peace', a different word. Voicing at the end keeps the request sounding polite and clear.
quests.mouthPosition: Hold your tongue tip near the ridge as for /s/, but keep the voice on until the very end. Let the buzz fade instead of chopping it off.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word starts with one of these sounds too, so focus only on the last sound. Stretch it: hiss alone, or hiss plus buzz?
quests.explanation: 'Size' begins with /s/ but ends with /z/, so both sounds are in the word and it's the ending that counts. The vowel stretches and the voice runs to the end. A hiss-only finish sounds clipped, and listeners may hear a different word or ask you to repeat.
quests.mouthPosition: Finish with the tongue tip near the ridge and your voice still on, letting a soft buzz carry to the end of the word.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Say the word and stop dead at the end. Which finish is quiet and clipped, with no voice left over?
quests.explanation: 'Seat' ends in /t/: the tongue tip closes on the ridge, the vowel stays fairly short, and the sound stops with no voice. With /d/ ('seed') the vowel stretches and a faint buzz continues. Listeners rely mostly on that vowel length.
quests.mouthPosition: Close the tongue tip on the ridge behind your upper teeth to stop the air; a tiny puff is optional, and no voice.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Freeze your tongue at the very end of the word. Is there still a hum in your throat while the back of your tongue is up?
quests.explanation: 'Leg' ends in /g/. The back of the tongue rises to the soft palate while the voice is still on and the vowel lingers a little. Drop the voice and you'd get 'lek', which isn't a word, so listeners have to guess from context. Keep the buzz.
quests.mouthPosition: Raise the back of your tongue to the soft palate at the end while your voice keeps going. Skip any strong puff.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Watch your lips as the word ends. Do they shut on a stretched, buzzy vowel or a short clipped one?
quests.explanation: 'Job' ends in /b/. The vowel is held a little longer and the voice continues into the closed lips, giving a soft finish. A voiceless /p/ ending would sound like 'jop' and leave the word less clear. Match the longer vowel with the buzz.
quests.mouthPosition: Close your lips at the end with the voice still running and let the sound fade without a pop.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The lips close in the middle of this word, between two vowels. As they open, do you feel a puff, or a soft voiced release?
quests.explanation: 'Paper' has /p/ at the start and again in the middle. In the middle, the lips close after the stressed syllable and open with a light puff before the second vowel. If the voice sneaks in, you get 'baper', a slip that's common when a sound falls between vowels.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'pay-', close both lips firmly, keep the throat quiet for a moment, then open into the short second vowel with a light puff.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Notice what happens right after the 'm' hum: the lips stay together. Is your voice on or off when they finally open?
quests.explanation: In 'number' the /b/ follows /m/. The lips are already closed for /m/, so you keep them shut, block the nose airflow, and release with the voice on. It's /b/ rather than /p/ because the voice never switches off between the two sounds.
quests.mouthPosition: Keep your lips closed after the 'm', block the air from your nose, then open them with your voice still running into the 'er'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle consonant is made with the back of your tongue. Is your throat buzzing as it lifts, tying the two syllables together?
quests.explanation: 'Tiger' has /g/ in the middle: the back of the tongue lifts to the soft palate while the voice stays on, then drops into the final 'er'. Swap in /k/ and you'd say 'ticker'. That buzz between vowels is the giveaway.
quests.mouthPosition: Lift the back of your tongue against the soft palate after 'tie-' with your voice on, then release into the short 'er' syllable.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Both sounds you're choosing between are in this word. Focus on the last one: does it keep a buzz right to the end?
quests.explanation: 'Five' begins with /f/ and ends with /v/. At the end the lip and teeth touch again, but the voice stays on and the vowel is fairly long. Speakers often soften the buzz there, but it should still be audible. Finish with /f/ and you've said 'fife'.
quests.mouthPosition: Bring your top teeth to your bottom lip at the very end and let a voiced buzz run through the gap before you stop.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Listen to the consonant right after the first stressed vowel. Put a finger on your lower lip: tickling or smooth?
quests.explanation: 'After' has /f/ in the middle, immediately followed by /t/. The lip-teeth hiss runs straight into a tongue-tip stop. Adding voice would give something like 'avter', which blurs the /f/ into the /t/. Keep the /f/ voiceless.
quests.mouthPosition: Once the 'a' is said, touch your top teeth to your bottom lip and let a voiceless stream out, then move your tongue tip up for the 't'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: In the middle of the word, your lip and teeth connect once. Does your voice stay on through that contact?
quests.explanation: 'Seven' has /v/ in the middle. The lip-teeth contact is voiced and links the two syllables. A voiceless version would sound like 'sefen'. The second syllable is short and weak, but the /v/ before it still needs its buzz.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'se-', bring your top teeth to your bottom lip with your voice on, then move quickly into the short 'n' ending.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Check whether your upper and lower lips meet at the start, or whether your bottom lip lands on your upper teeth.
quests.explanation: 'Vote' begins with /v/: the lower lip rests on the top teeth and a voiced stream of air runs through a small gap. /b/ closes both lips fully and releases with a pop. Mixing them turns 'vote' into 'boat', a serious change of meaning.
quests.mouthPosition: Put your top teeth on your bottom lip, switch your voice on, and let the air buzz through the gap: no lip closure, no pop.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: In the middle of the word, do both lips seal completely for a moment, or does air keep leaking through a gap?
quests.explanation: 'Habit' has /b/ in the middle: both lips seal fully and open in a quick voiced release. /v/ would leave a gap with air buzzing continuously and turn 'habit' into 'havit'. A complete closure is the feature to check.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'ha-', close both lips fully with your voice on and release lightly into 'it'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Both sounds are in this word. Focus only on the very first consonant: do your lips seal, or does a gap form?
quests.explanation: 'Believe' starts with /b/ and ends with /v/, so it trains you to keep the two apart by position. The opening is a full lip closure with a soft pop; the ending is a lip-teeth buzz. Swap them and the word becomes hard to recognise.
quests.mouthPosition: Begin with both lips sealed and release with a soft voiced pop, saving the lip-on-teeth buzz for the end of the word.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle of this word is spelled with an S. Say it slowly: does your throat buzz there, or is it a crisp hiss?
quests.explanation: 'Cousin' has /z/ in the middle even though it's written with S. Voicing tends to carry on between vowel-like sounds, so the buzz is natural here. A hiss would make the word sound stiff and slightly foreign.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'cou-', put your tongue tip near the ridge and let a voiced buzz run through it before the short 'in'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Focus on the sound in the middle. With a finger on your lower lip, is there tickling or just smooth air?
quests.explanation: 'Muffin' has /f/ in the middle: two Fs in the spelling, but a single voiceless hiss in the sound. Add voice and you get 'muvvin', which loses the crisp lip-teeth hiss. Keep your throat quiet between the vowels.
quests.mouthPosition: Following the first syllable, rest your top teeth on your bottom lip and blow voiceless air, then move on to 'in' quickly.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Stretch the last sound in the word. If your throat joins in, that's your clue.
quests.explanation: 'Face' ends in /s/, a voiceless hiss after a fairly short vowel. Voice it and you get 'phase', a real word that means something different. The two words differ only in that ending.
quests.mouthPosition: End with a clean hiss over the tongue tip with your voice off, and stop the air instead of fading into a buzz.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The tongue tip touches the ridge before the vowel. How much air escapes when it lets go: a clear puff, or almost none?
quests.explanation: 'Town' begins with /t/, a voiceless stop: a crisp tongue-tip tap followed by a burst of air. Voice it and you get 'down', an everyday mix-up when giving directions. Keep that opening burst firm.
quests.mouthPosition: Tap the tongue tip firmly on the ridge behind your top teeth and release with a small puff. Throat quiet until 'ow'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE END OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The word closes with your lip and teeth. Is your voice still buzzing at the moment they touch?
quests.explanation: 'Move' ends in /v/ even though the spelling stops at E. The voice runs through the long vowel into a lip-teeth buzz. Turn it into /f/ and it becomes 'moof', which no English word uses, so the word sounds clipped.
quests.mouthPosition: Round your lips for the 'oo', then bring your top teeth to your bottom lip at the end with your voice on.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Between the two syllables, the tongue tip forms a narrow channel. Is your voice quiet or on during it?
quests.explanation: 'Person' has a voiceless /s/ in the middle, right after the stressed vowel and /r/. Some learners voice it into /z/ before the weak ending, but it stays a hiss. The final syllable is short and blurred; the /s/ in front of it is what needs clarity.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'per-', bring your tongue tip near the ridge and blow a voiceless hiss before the short 'n'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: After the stressed syllable, the tongue tip taps the ridge and the word closes with a nasal. Was your voice on when the tongue tapped?
quests.explanation: 'Garden' has /d/ in the middle: the tongue tip presses the ridge with the voice on, and the release goes straight into a nasal 'n' with no vowel between. A voiceless /t/ would sound like 'garten'. The buzz keeps it clear.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'gar-', tap your tongue tip on the ridge with your voice on, then leave the tongue there and let air pass through your nose.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND AT THE START OF THE WORD
quests.hint: Say only the first sound for two seconds with a hand on your throat. Is there any vibration?
quests.explanation: 'Safe' starts with /s/: a voiceless hiss over the tongue tip. The ending is /f/, another voiceless hiss, so the word is a chain of two quiet sounds. A voiced start would give 'zafe'.
quests.mouthPosition: Hold your tongue tip close to the ridge and blow a thin voiceless stream, lips slightly spread for the 'ay'.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONSONANT SOUND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORD
quests.hint: The middle consonant follows a strong 'r' sound. Does it come with a puff of air as the lips open, or without one?
quests.explanation: 'Carpet' has /p/ right after /r/: the lips close and open with a small puff and no voice. Because the voice is already running through the 'r', learners often let it continue into /b/ and say 'carbet'. Switch the throat off for the closure.
quests.mouthPosition: After 'car-', close your lips with your voice off and release with a light puff into the short 'it'.
